content: Pulpitis refers to the inflammation of the dental pulp, which is the innermost part of the tooth containing nerves, blood vessels, and connective tissue. Causes of Pulpitis Pulpitis can occur when dental caries penetrate through the enamel and dentin, eventually reaching the pulp. Repeated dental procedures or trauma to the tooth can also lead to pulpitis. Regardless of the cause, the inflammation is often associated with bacterial infection. For instance, when a carious lesion breaches the pulp cavity, the tooth loses its protective seal against infectious pathogens. Similarly, if the blood supply to the pulp is compromised, bacteria can invade and colonize the pulp tissue. When the pulp becomes inflamed, pressure builds up within the pulp cavity. This pressure exerts force on the tooth's nerve and surrounding tissues, leading to varying degrees of pain, from mild discomfort to severe, excruciating pain. In some cases, the pressure can be so intense that the individual struggles to pinpoint the exact source of the pain, often mistaking it for pain in adjacent teeth. The unique anatomy of the pulp cavity complicates the resolution of inflammation. Unlike other parts of the body where pressure can dissipate through surrounding soft tissues and lymphatic drainage, the pulp cavity is encased in hard dentin. This rigid structure prevents the dissipation of pressure, increasing the likelihood of pulp necrosis if the inflammation persists. Furthermore, the pulp cavity presents a significant challenge to the immune system, making it highly unlikely for the body to eliminate a bacterial infection in this area without intervention. Once the pulp tissue dies, the pain may subside, but the infection can spread to surrounding anatomical structures, potentially leading to more severe complications. Differential Diagnosis of Pulpitis Pulpitis can be classified into two categories based on its clinical presentation and prognosis: 1. Reversible Pulpitis In this condition, the pulp remains vital and can recover once the irritant is removed. The inflammation does not cause permanent damage to the pulp tissue. 2. Irreversible Pulpitis In this case, the pulp is irreversibly damaged, and necrosis is inevitable. Pain may persist even after the removal of the irritant. The pain can vary in nature, being sharp, dull, or throbbing. If there is any drainage from the pulp cavity, the severity of the pain may decrease. However, the damage to the pulp is permanent. Treatment For reversible pulpitis, removing the irritant and addressing the underlying cause (e.g., treating caries) can allow the pulp to heal. For irreversible pulpitis, the following treatment options are available: Endodontic Therapy (Root Canal Treatment): The inflamed or necrotic pulp is removed, and the pulp chamber and root canals are cleaned, shaped, and filled with a biocompatible material such as gutta-percha. This procedure preserves the tooth structure. Tooth Extraction: If there is insufficient coronal tooth structure remaining to support a restoration after root canal therapy, extraction of the tooth may be necessary. Both treatment options aim to eliminate pain, prevent the spread of infection, and restore oral health.
